verdicts.reasoning: The short form, 'Order on Motion to Enforce Judgment', is the standard CM/ECF short description for an order that rules on a motion to enforce judgment. The long form is a minute order signed by Judge Sooknanan on 9/29/2026. It DENIES the Plaintiffs' 128 Motion to Enforce Summary Judgment Order. The summary judgment order is the judgment, so 'Motion to Enforce Judgment' is the event-type name for the same motion 128 that the judge names in prose. The two forms record the same kind of event (an order), act on the same motion, and fall on the same day (both entry_at 2026-09-29). The short form names no party, so there is no party conflict, and it names nothing the long form does not do. The long form also vacates the July 20 minute order. That is extra content in the same order, not a sign of a different event; short descriptions usually name only the motion being resolved. Both objects are unnumbered (entry_number null), as a D.D.C. minute order would be. One copy came from a timed source (time_filed 17:25:32, created 14:36 PDT) and the other from the docket text (time_filed null, created 16:31 PDT). A separate written order would normally have its own entry number. The window (9/28 to 9/30) has no other order and no other ruling on a motion to enforce. Its only other object is entry 149, a Notice of Supplemental Authority filed by the defendants on 9/28, which is not an order. No better match.

The window runs from 9/28 through 9/30 and holds three objects: the short form 479853687, the long form 479868690, and numbered entry 149 (479691487). That leaves the long form as the only order in the window, and it is exactly the order the short form names: the 9/29 minute order DENIES Plaintiffs' 128 Motion to Enforce Summary Judgment Order. It also vacates the July 20 status-report minute order, but that ruling is in the same docket text, not a separate entry that could compete. The window has no second order, minute entry or notice on 9/29 or 9/30. Both objects are unnumbered, which fits a D.D.C. minute order (no document number). The short form's time_filed is 17:25:32 on 9/29, and the long form was created in CourtListener later that day (16:31 PDT), on the signing date. The creation times are about two hours apart, not minutes, but that does not create another candidate. The long form is the only entry in the window that the short form can describe.

Read as a clerk would, the short form '.Order AND ~Util - Set/Reset Deadlines' is a plain Order event docketed together with the Set/Reset Deadlines utility event. It is not an 'Order on Motion', so it describes an order that rules on nothing and sets deadlines. The long form is that kind of order. It is an unnumbered MINUTE ORDER that grants or denies nothing. It sets Plaintiffs' response to the 116 Motion to Stay for 7/6/2026 at 5:00 PM and the Federal Defendants' reply for 7/7/2026 at 5:00 PM, and that is the Set/Reset Deadlines part. Both parts of the short form are things the long form does. The short form names nothing the long form does not do: no motion ruling, no hearing, no filing by a party. Both objects are unnumbered, which fits a minute entry. They are from the same day: the short form's time_filed is 08:53:52 on 7/2, and the long form was signed on 7/2/2026. That is the morning after the 116 motion was filed at 23:34 on 7/1, which is when a briefing-schedule order like this would plausibly issue. The long-form object has no time_filed and was created in CourtListener at about 16:22 ET. That is hours later, but it fits a later capture of the same minute entry from a source without times, and nothing in either text puts the order at a different time. The window holds no other order on 7/1-7/3. #116 (469510736) is the motion itself and #117 (469607476) is a notice of appearance, so neither fits the short form. The short form's type is generic, but its Set/Reset Deadlines part matches what the long form actually does, and the window has no other order that day for it to belong to. So it reads as the same minute entry.
